subject: Interpretation of Latent Response Fitted Means in an Ordinal CFA

messages.author: fc93c984d0ef2952
messages.subject: Interpretation of Latent Response Fitted Means in an Ordinal CFA
parts:
When we fit a CFA model in a measurement model with ordinal indicators, I get that we are trying to reconstruct the observed polychoric (in the case of polytomous variables) correlation matrix. In a model using the delta parametrization constraints, the fitted.values() command returns our model-implied matrix, the means (of the assumed latent normal variables) and the thresholds.

My question is, how can these fitted latent means be interpreted? How can we evaluate the fit of these means, is there a transformation that would make it comparable to the original ordinal scale (assuming that means of Likert items are interpretable)? Is the interpretation dependent on the level of constraints, in the context of a measurement invariance test?

Thank you in advance

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Interpretation of Latent Response Fitted Means in an Ordinal CFA
parts: In a model using the delta parametrization constraints, the fitted.values() command returns our model-implied matrix, the means (of the assumed latent normal variables) and the thresholds.
Regardless of parameterization, fitted() returns the model-implied polychoric correlations, standardized means, and standardized thresholds.
how can these fitted latent means be interpreted?
Means of standardized variables are always 0.
How can we evaluate the fit of these means

We can only fit a model to reproduce what we observed.  With categorical items, we are only reproducing the estimated polychoric correlations and standardized thresholds that we "observe", not any latent means or variances.
is there a transformation that would make it comparable to the original ordinal scale (assuming that means of Likert items are interpretable)?

No, if you want to use treat the numerical weights of your Likert scale as meaningful, you treat the items as numeric rather than as ordinal.

The mean vector is returned only because it is possible to have both continuous and categorical indicators in the same model, in which case there could be nonzero model-implied means for continuous variables, which do factor into the least-squares fit function.
Is the interpretation dependent on the level of constraints, in the context of a measurement invariance test?

Model parameters can imply different latent-response scales across contexts, assuming sufficient constraints on thresholds.  But regardless of the response scales implied by the model parameters, all model-implied covariance matrices are standardized for the categorical variables, as well as their thresholds, since we can only calculate the discrepancy between those and the "observed" counterparts that are also standardized.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Interpretation of Latent Response Fitted Means in an Ordinal CFA
parts: 1. You say 'means of standardized variables are always 0', but in a threshold invariant model where only the first group has scaling factors constrained to zero, the other groups are non-zero. Are these latent means standardized with the standard deviation of the first group?

Scaling factors are not means; they are the reciprocal of the marginal SD.

https://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/CatMGLong.pdf

Means of standardized variables are 0 because you subtract the mean; the SD is irrelevant.
1. I am not sure I capture what you mean by the "standardized thresholds that we "observe"", aren't the thresholds as unobserved as the latent response variable's variance or mean?
Yes, that's why I put "observed" in quotation marks.  They are estimates, but they are treated as observed data (which is why we need robust SEs and test statistics).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
